question: An oil or vacuum recloser is tested under:
explanation: Reclosers and sectionalizers have their own procedure. The trip-time table for molded-case breakers does not become the recloser’s curve. Control wiring, insulation, and contact resistance are still in 7.24.1, with limits that rhyme with breakers.

question: Recloser control wiring, ATS 7.24.1, shall not be less than:
explanation: 7.24.1.D.4 sets control-wiring insulation resistance at not less than 2 MΩ, the same floor used on breaker control circuits. Power-pole insulation is judged separately.

question: Insulating liquid in an oil recloser is judged against:
explanation: ATS 7.24.1 points the liquid at Table 100.4, the same family of limits used for new insulating oil. Do not grade recloser oil with a breaker timing table.

question: ATS 7.24.2 tests an automatic line sectionalizer’s counting function with simulated fault current:
choices: Below 10 percent of its continuous rating
Greater than 160 percent of its continuous current rating
explanation: The sectionalizer is proved by counting that current, locking out at each count position, and checking reset timing. It is not graded on a molded-case thermal curve. The insulating liquid, when it is an oil unit, is sampled and tested, not assumed to be a particular construction.

question: The insulating medium inside a 27 kV recloser is determined by:
choices: Assuming vacuum bottles under oil for every unit at that voltage
The nameplate, with the test procedure for that construction
explanation: Oil reclosers are sampled to Table 100.4. Vacuum units follow the vacuum checks when the manufacturer is silent. The construction is whatever the nameplate says. Do not assume one medium for every 27 kV unit.

question: Testing an automatic line sectionalizer under ATS 7.24.2, lockout is verified:
choices: At the count printed on the control door
explanation: The sectionalizer must lock out correctly for every count setting it can take. Reset timing is also verified. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.24.2.B.7.

question: Insulating liquid from an oil recloser is sampled. ATS 7.24.1 lists which dielectric breakdown method?
explanation: The recloser fluid list calls for dielectric breakdown by ASTM D877, plus the other fluid tests in the procedure. D924 is the power-factor method. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.24.1.B.5.

question: ATS 7.24.1's dielectric withstand step for an oil or vacuum recloser (no manufacturer data) sends you to which table?
explanation: Even though ATS has a recloser hipot table (100.15), the 7.24.1 withstand step points to Table 100.19 when the manufacturer is silent. MTS 7.24.1 does the same. Read the procedure, not just the table list. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.24.1.B.11; ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 7.24.1.

question: Compare the recloser hipot tables for a 14.4 kV-class recloser rated 15.5 kV maximum, 110 kV BIL. ATS Table 100.15 versus MTS Table 100.15:
choices: 35 kV at acceptance; 26.2 kV for maintenance
37.5 kV at acceptance; 50 kV for maintenance
explanation: The MTS value is the acceptance value with a 0.75 factor applied, rounded down. The 35/26.2 pair belongs to the 15.0 kV, 95 kV BIL row. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.15; ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Table 100.15.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.15; ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Table 100.15

question: For a 14.4 kV-class line sectionalizer, the 15-minute dc withstand in the sectionalizer tables is:
choices: 39 kV in ATS; 53 kV in MTS
78 kV in ATS; 58.5 kV in MTS
53 kV in ATS; 39 kV in MTS
explanation: ATS lists 35 kV ac / 53 kV dc and MTS lists 26.2 kV ac / 39 kV dc. The 78/58.5 pair belongs to the 24.9 kV class. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.16; ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Table 100.16.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.16; ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Table 100.16

question: A recloser's fast curve crosses a 20 A tap fuse's minimum-melt curve at about 800 A. A fault downstream of the fuse draws 1500 A. With a conventional C37.230 fuse-saving scheme, what happens, and what does partial-range fuse saving change?
choices: The recloser always clears first, so the fuse is saved at any current
Only the fuse operates, because fast curves are blocked above pickup
Both lock out, because fuse saving turns off reclosing

Above the crossing, the fuse melts and the recloser fast curve trips too, so every customer gets a momentary and the fuse is not saved. Partial-range saving caps the fast curve near 800 A so faults above it are left to the fuse
explanation: Fuse saving works only where the recloser fast curve is below the fuse minimum-melt curve. C37.230 explains that above the crossing both devices operate. The fuse is lost anyway and the whole feeder sees a needless momentary. Partial-range fuse saving limits the fast curve's response near the crossing current, so faults above it go to the fuse while the recloser holds on its slow curve. Source: IEEE C37.230-2020, 5.2.1 and 5.2.2; ANSI/NETA ETT-2026, 8.4.2.H.4 and 8.4.2.H.6.

question: Identify the device in the photo. It mounts on a pole or in a substation and is wired to a separate electronic control cabinet.
explanation: This is a three-phase recloser: three encapsulated poles on a common mechanism housing, run by an electronic control that trips it on a fault and recloses it. Eaton describes the NOVA as a three-phase, vacuum-interrupting recloser with solid epoxy-encapsulated interrupters, installed on poles or in substations. A sectionalizer can look similar, so use the model documentation rather than the number of poles alone to identify the device.
reference: Manufacturer product page: Eaton NOVA three-phase recloser, eaton.com; per manufacturer data
image_alt: Three gray insulated poles with sheds standing on a long gray mechanism housing.

question: ATS 7.24.1's visual and mechanical inspection of an oil or vacuum recloser includes mechanical operation and contact alignment tests. What are they done on, and what are they judged against?
choices: The recloser and its operating mechanism, against the manufacturer's published data
The control cabinet only, against Table 100.1
The recloser only, against the 50 percent rule
explanation: Both the recloser and its operating mechanism get mechanical operation and contact alignment checks, and the results are held to the manufacturer's data. Exercise the mechanism before you trust the electronic control. The 50 percent rule is for bolted connections and contact resistance, Table 100.1 is insulation resistance, and Table 100.19 is the withstand table. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.24.1.A.5 and C.1.

question: Which of these is on the ATS 7.24.1 visual and mechanical list for an oil recloser?
choices: Verify the insulating liquid level, held to the manufacturer's tolerances
Verify blade penetration and travel stops
Record the as-found and as-left operation counter readings
explanation: Liquid level is a recloser inspection item, judged against the manufacturer's recommended tolerances. Racking belongs to drawout breakers, blade penetration and travel stops to open air switches, and the counter readings show up on the vacuum breaker and air switch lists, not the 7.24.1 inspection list. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.24.1.A.7 and C.3; 7.6.3.A.10 and A.15; 7.5.1.3.A.7 and A.14.

question: A recloser tripped four times on a permanent fault and has stopped reclosing. What state is it in, and how does it get back to its normal sequence?
choices: Lockout; it needs a local or supervisory close, and then a reset interval before the full sequence is available again
Hold-closed; it will reclose by itself after 5 minutes
Failed; the vacuum bottles must be replaced
Lockout; it will reclose automatically once the fault clears
explanation: After running through all its programmed operations without restoring the circuit, a recloser goes to lockout, which blocks any more reclosing. Lockout can also be set locally or over SCADA. Leaving lockout takes a local or supervisory close command, and then the resetting interval has to run before the count is back to the full number of operations. Three reclose intervals (four trips) is the usual industry sequence. Source: IEEE C37.60-2018, Annex F, F.4 b) through d).
reference: IEEE C37.60-2018, Annex F, F.4 b) through d)

question: Why would a utility use a three-phase recloser rather than three single-phase reclosers on a feeder serving large three-phase motors?
choices: A three-phase recloser locks out all three phases on a permanent fault, so the motors aren't left single-phasing
Single-phase reclosers can't interrupt fault current
Three-phase reclosers don't need a control
Single-phase reclosers aren't made above 15 kV
explanation: Single-phase reclosers can lock out only the faulted phase and keep the other two phases in service, which suits mostly single-phase load. Three-phase motors would then run single-phased. A three-phase recloser locks out all three phases for a permanent fault. Source: IEEE C37.60-2018, Annex F, F.3.
